angle: The pilot corrected the court and the checker kept pace: a rebuilt 99 that convenes its engine more often (39.6% by turn 6, up from 34.3%) and closes slower (wincon access down to 42.6%), documented in five stamped case files — two of which exist to kill an infinite: one the database's, one our own.

teases: APPROACH OF THE SECOND SUN: the second-cast win, walked to the letter
7 DAMAGE A ROTATION, ZERO MANA — the punisher clock, checker-stamped
THE REBUILD: four new cards, 10,000 fresh goldfish games, one honest cost
DISPLACER KITTEN, AUDITED: unbounded casts survive. Unbounded mana does not.

departments.note: Heliod at hero scale from the pilot's actual printing, art by Victor Adame Minguez — credit line under the art per the featured-artist convention. The tagline 'Everyone draws. Everyone pays.' is the angle in four words; keep it directly under the deck name. This is Vol. 004 updated in place for the corrected build (HISTORY.md, sha 519adaa60d06): the dominant coverline sells the issue's signature, the refutation pair — A-001 kills the database's two-card infinite, A-005 kills our own hope that Displacer Kitten makes the loop mana-positive. Both are checker-passed fact, so the cover can promise both without inflation. Do not add a third violator, and do not tease the Aetherflux kill: it is unverified and the cover may not promise it.

Two-bucket contents plus the tier legend printed in full — Vol. 004, but every issue is somebody's first. In the THIS ISSUE'S DECK bucket, the one-line promise for The Kill should read 'three verified lines and two famous fakes' so the double refutation is promised from page two. departments.headline: THE GENEROSITY TRAP
departments.dek: Why would a control deck hand every opponent an extra card, every turn, on purpose — and then add a rabbit who gives them life too? Because in this court the cards aren't a gift. They're evidence, and the sentence is read at each opponent's upkeep.

callouts.title: LOOK LIKE A GIFT
callouts.text: Turns one through three are Remora into rock into Kami — or now Kwain, whose tap hands everyone a card and a life and makes the whole table like you. Eighteen lands plus nine rocks keep you on schedule while the pod files you under harmless, and every card an opponent accepts inches them toward the punisher thresholds.

callouts.title: LAND THE HINGE
callouts.text: Heliod arrives on turn 4 in the majority of simulated games — 5,165 of 10,000 on turn 4 exactly, 90.8% by turn 6. The front face rebuys an enchantment on arrival; the {3}{U/P} flip is the moment the deck turns on, and it can only ever happen at sorcery speed.

callouts.title: OPEN THE COURT
callouts.text: The Warped Eclipse grants everything flash and discounts your spells {1} for each card your opponents drew this turn. Your own Mines pay your mana bill — and the new hug layer feeds it on demand: a Kwain activation or a Second Doctor end-step offer grows the discount on exactly the turn you want to act.

callouts.title: PASS SENTENCE
callouts.text: The punishers convert hand size into upkeep damage: once Forced Fruition has filled a hand, cleanup trims it to exactly seven and the next upkeep costs them 7 — verified, repeating every rotation without you tapping a land. And 7 is now the floor: The Second Doctor removes the cleanup trim entirely, so hoarded hands just keep paying. When the court can't convene, Approach of the Second Sun is the clean exit.

captions.Howling Mine: **THE BAIT:** an extra card for everyone at each draw step. Perfectly symmetric on its face — the punishers and Heliod's discount are what make it yours.
captions.Kwain, Itinerant Meddler: **THE HANDSHAKE:** everyone draws, drawers gain a life, and the table likes you — while every accepted card feeds the punisher math and Heliod's discount. Two mana buys the waiting turns this deck lives on.
captions.Forced Fruition: **THE DETONATOR:** every opponent spell becomes seven forced draws. Nobody stays under the punisher threshold once this resolves.

pilot_tips.text: Check your opener for Leyline of Anticipation — it comes down free before turn one and makes every engine piece a flash play, which is Heliod's back face a full three turns early.

departments.pull_quote: The cards aren't a gift. They're evidence.

departments.headline: THEIR DRAWS, YOUR DISCOUNT
departments.dek: Your commander is the one card you are guaranteed to have — so what is that worth when the card is a hinge the whole deck turns on? Here, it is the single most reliable event in 10,000 simulations, and the tax math has a wrinkle no other deck in this series has had.
departments.body: Start with the guarantee. The command zone means Heliod is not a card you hope to draw: he is face up before the first mulligan is offered, and the simulator confirms what guaranteed access is worth — mean cast turn 4.098, median 4, down by turn 6 in 90.8% of games, the most dependable number in the whole issue. That is why Keep or Ship never asks your opening hand for a commander, an engine payoff or a win condition: the deck's hinge is already on the table, and your seven cards only need to buy the turns before him. The tax ladder reads 4, then 6, then 8, then 10 — but this commander's real recast cost is the wrinkle: Heliod always returns front-face-up, so every recast is tax PLUS another {3}{U/P} PLUS another sorcery-speed window you may never safely get. That math is why protection beats recasting here more decisively than usual — the commander-insurance spend is Lightning Greaves through the flip window and a counterspell held for the removal, because you are not protecting a 4/4, you are protecting a transform activation you cannot take reactively. Color identity is its own lesson: the front face is mono-white, but a double-faced card's identity is the union of its faces, and the blue back face is the entire reason this is a WU deck — the operating color, too: 50 blue pips across 35 cards against 14 white pips across 13. The 21-damage clock, for once, is a coincidence: a 4/4 needs six connections and this deck plans zero of them. And the political read: the Radiant Dawn resolving next to a Kwain looks like the friendliest board in the format, and the table will treat it that way — but a turn-one Rhystic Study tells every experienced pilot what bracket you actually are, because this list's floor is 4 on the strength of eight Game Changers alone. The zone guarantees the hinge; the format guarantees the tell.

captions.Heliod, the Radiant Dawn // Heliod, the: **THE HINGE:** the front face rebuys an enchantment on arrival; the {3}{U/P} flip — sorcery speed only, 2 life if you're short a blue — makes your whole deck flash and bills your spells to the table's draw count.
captions.Lightning Greaves: **THE INSURANCE:** shroud through the flip window costs two mana. An answered Heliod costs tax, another {3}{U/P}, and a sorcery window you may never get back.

pilot_tips.text: Equip the Greaves the turn you plan to flip, not the turn Heliod lands — the transform is the one action this deck can never take reactively, so it is the thing worth insuring.

departments.pull_quote: You are not protecting a 4/4. You are protecting a sorcery-speed activation you only get to take while he lives.

departments.headline: THE REBUILD, MEASURED
departments.dek: We ran the corrected 99 another 10,000 times on seed 42 and the ledger is honest in both directions: the engine got more reliable, and the deck got slower at ending things. Both numbers are on this page, uncooked.

callouts.title: 74.2% KEEPABLE
callouts.text: 74.2% of first sevens are keeps at 0.326 mulligans per game. Eighteen lands sounds reckless until you see the kept-hand distribution centered on 2–3 lands plus rocks — the nine mana rocks are load-bearing, not filler.

callouts.title: TURN 4, LIKE CLOCKWORK
callouts.text: The commander histogram spikes at turn 4 — 5,165 of 10,000 games — with mean 4.098 and 90.8% by turn 6. Heliod is the most reliable event in the deck; the plan can afford patience everywhere else because the hinge shows up on a date.

callouts.title: WHAT THE REBUILD BOUGHT: 39.6%
callouts.text: 'Engine + punisher assembled', the deck's core two-piece, now lands by turn 6 in 39.6% of games, up from 34.3% before Kwain and The Second Doctor joined the engine count — 54.8% ever, mean turn 4.2. Better, and still a minority: in most games you are a draw-go control deck waiting for the court to convene.

callouts.title: WHAT IT COST: 42.6%
callouts.text: Win-condition access by turn 6 fell to 42.6% with White Sun's Zenith moved to the sideboard pool. The deck got more consistent at its engine and thinner at closing — which is why Mystical Tutor and Long-Term Plans now carry more weight than any single wincon slot.

callouts.title: SAYING NO IN 73.3%
callouts.text: Free or cheap interaction is in hand by turn 6 in 62.2% of games and 73.3% overall — nearly identical to the keep rate. Holding up an answer is not a fallback plan; it is the statistically dominant line.

captions.Thought Vessel: **LAB NOTE:** rocks contribute from the turn after they land in this model — and mean available mana still hits 4.238 on turn 4 and 4.965 on turn 5. Heliod on four, the flip on five: the schedule pays for itself.

pilot_tips.text: Lead Ancient Tomb into a two-mana rock whenever the opener offers it — that line is how 27.8% of simulated games put Heliod down by turn 3.

departments.pull_quote: The rebuild bought consistency at the engine and paid for it in closing speed. Both numbers, no rounding.
departments.note: The stated-assumptions box is non-negotiable and this issue it earns its keep twice: the model simulates resource development, not games — and it does not model cost reducers, which means every number on this page ignores Heliod's discount entirely. The real deck is faster than the chart; the chart is the floor. Say exactly that, in the lab voice. Cite the sha (519adaa60d06) so nobody mistakes these for the previous build's figures.

departments.headline: COURT IS IN SESSION
departments.dek: Five lines went to the adversarial checker and five came back stamped. Two win the game, one is an engine that wins nothing on its own — and two are refutations: the database's famous infinite, and our own best idea about the cat.

callouts.title: THE TRIGGER SITS ON TOP
callouts.text: The default win, under fire: an opponent aims Naturalize at Forced Fruition, and the Fruition trigger goes on the stack above the very spell that caused it. They draw their seven cards before the enchantment dies — the ability resolves no matter what happens to its source. FULL DOSSIER: JUDGE'S DESK A-003.

callouts.title: CLEANUP DOES YOUR HOMEWORK
callouts.text: At the end of their turn, the cleanup step trims that inflated hand back to exactly seven cards — which happens to be precisely the threshold both punishers want. You did not spend a card or a mana on this part.

callouts.title: SEVEN AT THE BELL
callouts.text: Next upkeep: Ebony Owl Netsuke sees seven-plus cards and deals 4; Iron Maiden deals hand-size-minus-four for 3. Seven damage, from you, with every land untapped — and that is the verified floor. With The Second Doctor removing everyone's maximum hand size, the trim never happens and a ten-card hand pays 6 to the Maiden instead of 3 while the Owl keeps firing.

callouts.title: BURY THE SUN, DIG IT UP
callouts.text: The clean exit: Approach of the Second Sun's first cast gains 7 life — 14 with Alhammarret's Archive out — and buries it seventh from the top, trivially shallow when everyone is drawing in bulk. Mystical Tutor at an end step puts it back on top on demand. FULL DOSSIER: JUDGE'S DESK A-002.

callouts.title: THE ONLY WINDOW
callouts.text: The second cast wins during resolution, as a spell effect — and the first casting still counts even though the card was shuffled away, because the game tracks the event, not the card. The table's one and only window is while the second Approach is on the stack; the case file plays out the counter-war, Swan Song included.

callouts.title: AN ENGINE, NOT A KILL
callouts.text: Hullbreaker Horror + Sol Ring + Arcane Signet is a verified unbounded-cast loop: each rock's cast bounces the other, and tapping each before it leaves keeps the cycle at exactly 3 mana in, 3 out. It nets no mana, no cards, no damage. The Aetherflux Reservoir exit is a candidate that still needs a stack scenario — we will not call it a kill until the checker does. And the two-card version 296,000 database decks believe in? Refuted. FULL DOSSIER: A-001 and A-004.

callouts.title: THE CAT DOESN'T PAY
callouts.text: The hope: Displacer Kitten blinks Sol Ring untapped mid-loop and the engine goes mana-positive. The verdict: no. Both triggers lock their targets at announcement, and whichever resolves first makes the other's target a new object — blink and bounce are mutually exclusive on every cast. Keep the loop and the Kitten adds nothing; blink first and the loop terminates, a one-time exit worth exactly 3 floating mana. Unbounded casts survive. Unbounded mana does not exist. FULL DOSSIER: A-005.

captions.Forced Fruition: **THE VERDICT DELIVERED:** seven forced draws per opponent spell — and the trigger resolves even when the spell that fired it is the removal that kills it.
captions.Ebony Owl Netsuke: **EXHIBIT A:** a flat 4 at each opponent's upkeep at seven-plus cards. Two mana, bought in 1996 money, dealing 2026 damage.
captions.Iron Maiden: **EXHIBIT B:** hand size minus four, computed on resolution — which means cards added in response to the trigger count against them.
captions.Approach of the Second Sun: **THE CLEAN EXIT:** the win is checked mid-resolution, not by state-based action. Once every player passes on the second cast, nothing in the game can stop it.
captions.Hullbreaker Horror: **THE ENGINE, AUDITED:** with Sol Ring alone, nothing — the trigger can't target your own spell on the stack. With Sol Ring plus a true two-mana rock, unbounded casts in one main phase.
captions.Displacer Kitten: **THE HOPE, AUDITED:** every noncreature cast blinks something — but never the thing the Horror is already bouncing. The loop stays 3-in, 3-out, and the Kitten's best trick is a one-time exit at 3 floating mana.

pilot_tips.text: Hold Swan Song for the counter-war on the second Approach — a 2/2 Bird is a bargain against winning the game, and the case file shows exactly where it slots into the stack.
Aim Stroke of Genius at the punished player while Iron Maiden's trigger is on the stack — the Maiden counts their hand on resolution, so every card you force is another point of damage.
Price any X exit off the verified ceiling: the Kitten-first ordering ends the loop with exactly 3 mana floating, so X is 3 plus whatever real mana you held — never the number the table fears.

departments.pull_quote: The clock runs during everyone else's draw step. Once it's live, your only job is protecting it.
departments.note: One feature spread per verified line, in this order: A-003 (the default win) gets the marquee scenario-box, A-002 second, A-004 third — then the refutation pair A-001 + A-005 as a linked double spread, because killing two infinites in one issue is the strongest credibility page this publication has printed. Citations stay in Judge's Desk; this department narrates. The Aetherflux exit is flagged 'needs a stack scenario' wherever it is mentioned — no exceptions. The Second Doctor extension in callout 3 is oracle text riding a verified line, not itself a case file; keep its phrasing coach-voiced.

departments.headline: GUILTY OF LOOKING HARMLESS
departments.dek: At a bracket-4 table the gift bow fools nobody for long — professional pods have seen Kwain before, and they know the genre. So which misreads survive, and how do you spend the ones that do?

callouts.title: THREAT WINDOW
callouts.text: Engine plus punisher on the battlefield with Heliod flipped: that is the board state that makes you archenemy, and once it exists you should embrace it openly — the verified clock deals 7 on each punished upkeep and re-arms every rotation without you tapping out. Before that board exists, stay small and boring: a lone Iron Maiden is ignored; a lone Howling Mine is welcomed.

callouts.title: THE LOUDEST TELLS
callouts.text: Forced Fruition resolving is a table-wide event that makes you archenemy immediately unless a punisher is already taxing the refill. And Mystical Tutor at an end step after your first Approach has resolved means exactly one thing to anyone who has done the reading — count the table's open blue, hold Dovin's Veto or Swan Song for the commit turn, never telegraph it a rotation early.

callouts.title: THE DOCTOR'S BARGAIN
callouts.text: The Second Doctor's end-step offer blanks the attack step of every opponent who accepts — a pillow fort three players pay for with cards that feed your Maiden anyway. Professionals do that math, accept it, and resent it: expect the deterrent to buy two to three real turns before someone eats the card loss to kill the Doctor. Those bought turns are the whole game now.

callouts.title: THE FALSE ALARM
callouts.text: With Displacer Kitten out, experienced opponents assume the worst about what your board does mid-stack — some tables still 'know' you as the Hullbreaker–Sol Ring infinite deck. Let them fear it; just don't believe it yourself. Case A-001 refuted the two-card line and A-005 capped the Kitten ceiling at 3 floating mana. The fear is worth more than the board. Spending removal on it is their mistake, not your plan.

captions.Rhystic Study: **THE BRACKET TELL:** turn-one Rhystic Study is priced in at this tier — it draws groans, not removal — but it tells every experienced pilot what the hug costume is hiding: an eight-Game-Changer, floor-4 list.
captions.Smothering Tithe: **REMOVED ON SIGHT:** at a professional table Tithe dies immediately or the pod pays in lockstep. Deploy it the rotation you can spend the treasure, never as a turn-2 flex.
captions.Consecrated Sphinx: **THE ARCHENEMY SWITCH:** this does not resolve quietly at tier 4. Land it when you can defend it — or when you are ready to be the threat on purpose.

pilot_tips.text: In the control mirror, say 'it can't be countered' out loud before you need it — the uncounterable wrath is a political instrument that redirects the board-committing player's aggression somewhere else.
Spend Teferi's Protection on the Farewell-class sweeper, not the alpha strike — it phases out your entire punisher board, which is the asset the attack was never going to touch.

departments.pull_quote: The table's fear of your Kitten board is worth more than the board itself. You know the ceiling is three.

departments.headline: TWO TABLES, NO TAKEBACKS
departments.dek: One turn asks whether generosity is safe with a spellslinger across the table; the other asks when a god should change faces. Read each board, commit out loud, and only then read the bench's ruling.

callouts.title: HOW TO PLAY ALONG
callouts.text: Cover the recommendation box with your hand. Read the board, pick a branch, say it out loud — the signals and coalition risks are printed with each branch precisely so you can argue with them. Being wrong on this page is free; being wrong at the table costs a game.

pilot_tips.text: Deploy Dictate of Kruphix at the end of the turn before the upkeep you most want taxed — flash means the extra draws start exactly where you point them.
Use Folio of Fancies' X-activation as a precision tool: push exactly the hand you want over seven, exactly when the punishers are about to ask.

departments.pull_quote: The flip is the one action this deck can never take reactively. Its risk compounds every cycle it waits.
departments.note: Two spreads from the decision artifacts: 001 (turn 6 — does Forced Fruition come down against a spellslinger?) and 002 (turn 7 — when does Heliod become the Warped Eclipse?). Both were re-authored against the corrected build and cite the current 519adaa6 goldfish figures — render them as current, verbatim. The recommendation must sit visually below the branches in both; neither dek nor headline may hint at the answers.

departments.headline: WHO BREAKS THE COURT
departments.dek: Creature wraths hit almost nothing you care about, and one archetype turns your own engine into their best card. Can you name the pod where the correct play is Kwain never tapping at all?

threats.read: This is the one. Your draw engines, all three punishers, nine mana rocks, Propaganda and Ghostly Prison sit in a single blast radius, while creature wraths hit a handful of utility bodies you can rebuild. Deploy the engine in layers instead of dumping it, bank countermagic for the one spell that takes the board, and remember Heliod's front face rebuys an enchantment on every recast. New this build: in the mirror, Supreme Verdict is YOUR reset — it wraths their Torrential Gearhulk board through open permission at zero counterspell cost, which flips who must commit first.
outs: Heliod, the Radiant Dawn // Heliod, the Warped Eclipse

threats.read: Be honest with yourself: your engine is their engine, and the hug layer is a liability here, not a politics play. Forced Fruition hands a storm pilot seven cards per spell, a tapped Kwain is a gift certificate to the one player who profits from raw cards, and The Second Doctor's offer goes to the other two seats only. Deploy the asymmetric layer instead — a turn-one Remora against a spell-dense pod is one of the best cards in your 99 — and spend the free suite by the answer-economy bar: counter the ritual engine or the payoff, never the cantrip.

Every deck that wins 'on resolution' has one interaction window exactly like your Approach does, and your job is knowing theirs as precisely as you know yours. Free counter on the enabler, Swords on the reanimated body, overloaded Rift when the window has already passed. The judgment flag: your forced draws fill delve and escape graveyards as a side effect — against those decks the Mine effects cost more than they look, and your own graveyard asks for nothing, so opposing hate is a shrug.

You are the control deck and happy about it. Propaganda, Ghostly Prison, and now The Second Doctor's rider each blank attack plans from three players — virtual card advantage tripled — and the punishers push an aggro deck's damage-per-card below what 40 life demands. Commit almost nothing to the board yourself and let them overextend into the uncounterable Supreme Verdict. The trap is sequencing: Forced Fruition into an empty aggro hand is a full refill of live threats, so land punishers before or with the big draw pieces.

pilot_tips.text: Against storm and spellslinger pods, hold Forced Fruition all game if you must — seven free cards per spell is a donation those decks convert faster than your punishers can tax it.
Against a known combo seat, Kwain stays untapped — the same activation that buys goodwill at an aggro table is a free card to the one player assembling a kill.

departments.pull_quote: Your engine is their engine. Whether that's a weapon or a liability is decided by who's sitting across from you.

departments.headline: ENGINES, PUNISHERS, AND THE LAW
departments.dek: Eighty-five cards doing six jobs: feed the table, tax the hand, buy the waiting turns, keep your own draws asymmetric, say no, or end it. The load-bearing cards lead — and the role histogram famously can't see half of them.

roster.role: The court: engines that feed the table
The hug fort: gifts with riders
The resets and the blink engine

captions.Alhammarret's Archive: **THE RIGGING:** your draws double, your lifegain doubles, and nobody else's do — Kwain pays you twice on both halves, and a first Approach banks 14. Five mana that turns every symmetric engine you run into a rigged one.
captions.The Second Doctor: **HEADS AND TAILS:** no maximum hand size means the cleanup trim never saves anyone from the Maiden — and each opponent who takes the end-step card can't attack you next turn. Heads they can't attack, tails they fall behind.
captions.Consecrated Sphinx: **THE MAGNET:** two cards to you per card an opponent draws — fourteen per opponent spell under Forced Fruition, and the strongest removal magnet you play.
captions.Temple Bell: **THE INSTANT-SPEED HUG:** a draw for everyone, on demand — ring it in response to removal for pure value, or to push a hand where the punishers want it.

pilot_tips.text: With Displacer Kitten out, any noncreature cast blinks Remora back as a new object with zero age counters — the cumulative upkeep restarts from nothing. The long-run value line is still a flagged candidate, but the object math is plain oracle text.

departments.note: Rank matters: the punisher core and the engines lead, mana closes. Say the honest structural fact out loud in the intro — 23 of these cards, including nearly the entire punisher core, have no entry in the role taxonomy, so anyone judging this list by a role histogram will conclude it has no plan. The histogram is wrong; the plan is on this page. The sideboard strip renders separately and now holds the rebuild's four cuts (Agent of Treachery, Chasm Skulker, United Front, White Sun's Zenith) alongside the refactoring pool — label it as the pool it is, per HISTORY.md. Tiles are role-first and carry no printing credits — the physical cards belong to Featured Artist.

departments.headline: A HUNDRED AND SEVEN HANDS
departments.dek: Nobody painted more than a handful of cards in this collection — 107 artists across 145 entries once the sideboard pool is counted, the flattest credits page in this series. So who leads a deck with no favorites, and what does a list like that tell you about how it was built?

featured.note: John Avon keeps the feature for the corrected build with three cards in the 99: Fellwar Stone, Mikokoro, Center of the Sea, and the Plains art. The raw ranking's top line now reads Adam Paquette at five entries — but look closely and two of those are the same river painted twice (two printings of Prairie Stream) and two more live in the sideboard pool, not the 99, which is exactly why this department reads the table instead of quoting it. Count per copy and you'd crown someone else again: the Island art appears eleven times and Avon's Plains six — repetition is printing, not authorship, so we count cards, always, and list copies as their own labeled fact. There is no Secret Lair run hiding in these numbers, no collector-number streak, no product bought whole: a hundred-plus artists across three decades of sets, from Mark Tedin's Braingeyser to this year's printings, is what a deck assembled one card at a time looks like. And if one Avon card earns the hero slot, it is Mikokoro, Center of the Sea — the whole issue's thesis painted onto a land: everyone gets a card, it can't be countered, and it survives every board wipe in the format.

also_worth_noting.note: Three cards, one of them the rebuild's quiet hinge: Alhammarret's Archive — the asymmetry doubler the correction added — beside Mana Confluence and Skyscribing.
Two cards, one lineage: Braingeyser and Temple Bell — the game's oldest everyone-draws job and its bell-shaped descendant, decades apart, same hand.
Both of the deck's flash haymakers are his: Hullbreaker Horror and Torrential Gearhulk, the two creatures that arrive mid-counter-war.

captions.Mikokoro, Center of the Sea: **THE THESIS, PAINTED:** John Avon's island hands every player a card — uncounterable, wrath-proof, and exactly what this deck is for.
captions.Braingeyser: **THE ELDER:** Mark Tedin's Braingeyser is the oldest job in the deck — force-feeding a hand past seven has been blue's business since the beginning.

departments.pull_quote: Repetition is printing, not authorship. We count the cards, not the copies.
departments.note: The analysis reports no standout (its own note: the lead artist has 5 cards — tell a breadth story) and an empty drop-run list — this is the breadth story the spec promises for exactly this case, told for the second time because the rebuild didn't change it. Art File fast-facts from the computed credits, labeled honestly: 145 entries / 166 copies / 107 artists across the 99 plus the 60-entry refactoring sideboard pool (the 99 itself is 85 entries, 100 copies); 1 foil, 1 borderless; top set Secrets of Strixhaven Commander at 9 entries by 9 different artists. The renderer recomputes all counts — this plan supplies only the choice and the prose.

departments.headline: FOUR OPENERS, FOUR RULINGS
departments.dek: The sim keeps 74.2% of first sevens, so the question is rarely whether to keep — it's which of these four you would ship anyway. Rule on each before you read the bench's reason.

hands.why: Three lands, a rock, an asymmetric engine, a table engine, and something that says no — the exact bar: two to four lands, one card-flow piece, an answer. Heliod needs no help from your seven; he arrives by turn 6 in 90.8% of games on his own.

Ancient Tomb into a two-mana rock is the deck's accelerant — the line behind the 27.8% of games that land Heliod by turn 3. Kwain now counts among the two-mana engines worth keeping a hand for: the table draws with you, likes you for it, and feeds the punisher math anyway.

hands.verdict: SHIP — a courtroom with no plaintiffs
hands.why: Three punishers and not one card that makes anybody draw. Iron Maiden against a normal five-card hand is one damage a turn — the punishers are inert until the engine exists, and this hand is a mulligan in costume. Two lands, no rock, no flow. Ship it.

Three lands and four cards that are all the back half of a game. Nothing here draws, taxes, or says no — and you never mulligan chasing Approach anyway: wincon access is 42.6% by turn 6 in the rebuilt list, and the correct response is trusting Mystical Tutor and Long-Term Plans to find it when the board is ready, not digging for it at hand-quality prices.

captions.Mystic Remora: **THE UPGRADE:** the card that turns a marginal keep into a live one — a turn-one Remora often banks three-plus cards before the upkeep bites.

pilot_tips.text: Pay Remora's cumulative upkeep two or three times, then let it go — the ages are a fee, not a mortgage, and the cards are already banked.

departments.pull_quote: You are mulliganing toward flow plus interaction — never toward the lock.

departments.headline: NOTHING OBSOLETES AN IRON MAIDEN
departments.dek: The obsolescence index has real opinions about this mana base, no idea what a punisher is for — and, this issue, an opinion about all four of the rebuild's new cards. We audited every entry, and the audit is the department.

pilot_tips.text: Make Worn Powerstone your first cut when trimming — it enters tapped, costs three, and the verified loop math already excludes it: the engine needs a castable two-drop that taps the turn it lands.
Ignore the index's Sol Ring comparison here — Fellwar's real demerit is the verified one: it sustains the Hullbreaker loop only while an opponent's land can actually produce mana.

The index says Mystical Tutor obsoletes it, but the supersession is narrower than it looks — Plans fetches permanents: a punisher, the Reservoir, the missing loop rock. Keep both until a slot is on fire.

The index's 'replacement' for the Archive is a pay-three, counter-limited single draw with no doubling clause. Read the oracle text and move on — the clause you added this card for has no printed substitute.
